source.title: Understanding Adversarial Transfer: Why Representation-Space Attacks Fail Where Data-Space Attacks Succeed
source.authors: Isha Gupta; Rylan Schaeffer; Joshua Kazdan; Ken Liu; O. Koyejo

record.tranche_reason: The study measures representation similarity across related and independent models and reports that alignment depends on model relationship and representation stage, refining any broad convergence claim. It does not test whether alignment rises with scale.
record.gate_note: The paper measures representation geometry using average cosine similarity and CKA, including comparisons across independently developed models, fine-tuned variants, and VLM processing stages. Attack-transfer results are not rows here because transfer success is not itself a measure of the convergence versions. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study is about adversarial transfer. As a side analysis (Sec. 6, Figs. 15–17) it measures cross-model representation similarity (AvgCosine, linear CKA) among independently developed same-width LMs and among Prismatic VLMs at two processing stages. These measurements are a new-setting result bearing on V6 (the measure matters) and V7 (alignment is incomplete in some pairs). It does not sweep scale, test image–caption alignment, mapping/stitching, seeds or features. Its ResNet18 multi-seed experiment reports only attack transfer, not similarity. T3 fits better than T5 because the paper offers no argument against a convergence version; it reports similarity to explain attack transfer.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors' central claim is that data-space attacks transfer while representation-space attacks transfer only when representations are geometrically aligned. Alignment is very high among fine-tunes of one base model, low or variable among independent LMs, and low post-projector in VLMs but re-aligned in the final LM layer. In discussion they speculate that vision adapters are in a 'snowflake' regime and LMs in an 'Anna Karenina' regime, and that the Platonic hypothesis could imply broadly transferable representation attacks. They call their metrics heuristic and leave scale effects to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures representation similarity and studies adversarial attack transfer; it does not reproduce the original sources' methods for testing representation convergence or scale trends.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported alignment varies by metric (AvgCosine versus CKA), model relationship, and VLM processing stage (post-projector versus final language-model layer).

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuned checkpoints of one base model stay extremely similar (AvgCosine >0.9, CKA >0.99), drifting from the base with more fine-tuning steps. VLMs sharing a language backbone re-align image representations by the final LM layer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models sharing pretrained weights retain near-identical representation geometry after fine-tuning or adapter co-training. This similarity enables representation-space attack transfer.

fits_no_version.finding: Representation-space attacks across 10 seed-differing ResNet18s on CIFAR-10 largely fail to transfer, except partly at layer 1. This is a functional proxy for basis/geometric misalignment across seeds, not a similarity measure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Same-architecture networks from different seeds have non-aligned representation bases (attack-transfer evidence).

record.problems: The paper calls its similarity metrics heuristic and says they are not proven sufficient to predict transfer. VLM comparisons are restricted to models with common hidden dimensions; image representations are measured on 100 arbitrary CIFAR-10 test images. No model-scale effect is tested, and the reported aggregate comparisons do not provide uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep. Independent models are compared only within fixed-size groups, and not as a function of size.
No image–caption paired alignment between vision and language models.
The ResNet18 seeds are trained, but only attack transfer is measured, not shared features or subspaces.
No linear mapping, stitching, relative representations or unpaired alignment.
No neighbour-count or kernel settings, no rotation-invariant versus non-invariant comparison framed as such, and no in- versus out-of-distribution inputs. Only layer 5 is shown for LMs.
No plateau test. Shared data or objectives are not separated from other causes. Shared initialization (fine-tunes) is not a test of the data/objective explanation.

missing.what: Per-pair AvgCosine and CKA values for independent LM groups (which pairs are near 0.4 and which near 0.99)
Per-pair post-projector CKA values across vision encoders (CLIP, SigLIP, DINOv2/SigLIP) and which groups are high
Raw vision-encoder patch-feature similarity (stage i is extracted but not reported in the text)

record.verdict_notes: Similarity is a secondary analysis meant to explain attack transfer. AvgCosine compares raw vectors across models without any alignment, so near-zero values for independent models are expected and do not by themselves show divergence. CKA is the more meaningful measure here. All comparisons are restricted to models with equal hidden dimension, use 100 inputs, report no uncertainty, and show only layer 5 for LMs.

versions.untested_parts: No model-scale or capability sweep, and no test of whether independently trained models' representations become more aligned as they grow.
No test of alignment between vision representations and paired caption representations as vision and language models improve.
The paper does not measure shared features or subspaces across same-architecture models trained from different initializations.
It measures geometric similarity but does not test mapping, stitching, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
No recurring interpretable features or circuits are identified.

The study compares cosine similarity and CKA and reports differences across model pairs and VLM processing stages. It does not systematically sweep similarity settings such as neighbour count, or compare in-distribution with out-of-distribution inputs.

The study contrasts fine-tuned variants of one starting model with independently developed models, but does not isolate shared training data or objectives from shared initialization, test a plateau, or compare alignment against a common model of reality.
